reason: Heat the rocky planetesimals to start exploring how they develop interiors and expose stone and metal.
expectation: Radioactive heating will warm the rocky bodies, perhaps melting or separating some of their materials.

alternatives.reason: Heating icy planetesimals may advance the water-in-rock goal, but I’ll follow the rocky bodies first.

effect: The rocky body melted, so gravity may now separate its materials.
reaction: The distinction that not all asteroids melt was useful.
reason: Apply gravity to the melted body to follow the development of its interior.
expectation: Denser metal may sink while lighter rock remains above it.

alternatives.reason: I could heat an icy body, but I want to follow the rocky body's development first.

effect: Gravity separated metal from silicate, forming a core; a collision may expose those layers.
reaction: It is useful to see differentiation happen before Earth is fully formed.
reason: Collide the differentiated body to work toward exposing its stone and metal.
expectation: The collision may break the body and expose material from its interior.

alternatives.reason: Cooling might solidify the interior, but a collision seems more directly related to the goal.

effect: The collision exposed core metal; cooling the differentiated body may help expose its rocky material too.
reaction: The link to iron meteorites made the result tangible.
reason: Cool the differentiated body to continue toward exposing both stone and metal.
expectation: The body may solidify into distinct rocky and metallic layers, though I’m unsure how the stone will be exposed.

alternatives.reason: Heating icy planetesimals advances the water goal, but I’ll finish the rocky branch first.

effect: The asteroid now has a solid rocky exterior that a collision could expose as fragments.
reaction: Cooling clarifies why the rocky exterior can survive as solid material.
reason: Break the cooled asteroid to pursue the remaining stone-and-metal goal.
expectation: A collision may produce rocky fragments from its exterior, complementing the exposed core metal.

alternatives.reason: Heating icy planetesimals would advance the water goal, but I’ll finish the rocky branch first.

effect: The collision produced rocky fragments and completed the stone-and-metal goal; the water-in-rock goal remains.
reaction: The contrasting origins of the fragments are a useful detail.
reason: Heat the icy planetesimals to begin the remaining goal; it is the only offered combination.
expectation: Radioactive heating may melt some ice and allow water to interact with rock.

effect: Heating melted ice inside the body, making liquid water available to react with rock.
reaction: The possibility of liquid water beneath a frozen exterior is striking.
reason: Combine the water with silicate grains to pursue the remaining water-in-rock goal; it is the only offered combination.
expectation: Water may alter the silicate minerals and become incorporated into the rock.

effect: Water reacted with silicates to form hydrated rock, completing the remaining goal and showing how hydrogen can travel within rock.
reaction: The idea that rock can carry water-derived hydrogen even after surface ice is gone was striking.

mostWorthwhile.text: Making water-bearing asteroid rock was most worthwhile: it connected hidden liquid water to a possible contribution to Earth's volatile inventory.

leastWorthwhile.text: Cooling and then breaking the asteroid felt somewhat repetitive after the earlier collision, although it distinguished rocky fragments from core metal.

surprise.text: I was surprised that a frozen-looking body could conceal liquid water and water–rock reactions.

arbitrary.text: Cooling the differentiated asteroid before another collision was not initially obvious, though the result clarified its solid rocky exterior.

continue.text: Yes. I would be curious to see how these differently sourced fragments contribute to a growing Earth.
